definition: Plyler v. Doe, 457 U.S. 202 (1982) is a United States Supreme Court case where the Court held that denying undocumented children access to a free public education violated the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. Background In May of 1975, a statute was enacted in the state of Texas that was intended to restrict undocumented children from attending public schools. The Texas legislature revised its education laws to:  Withhold state funds from local school districts that provided education to children who were not “legally admitted” into the United States; and  To authorize local school districts to deny enrollment to children who were not lawfully residing in the United States. The broad issue presented to the Court was whether the Texas statute violated the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The Equal Protection Clause provides that no state shall “deny to any person within its jurisdiction the equal protection of the laws.” In reaching a decision in this case, the Court addressed three principal questions. Arguments and Holdings The Court first considered whether undocumented immigrants are “persons within the jurisdiction” of a state and therefore entitled to protection under the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. Texas argued that, because undocumented individuals were present in the country in violation of federal immigration law, they were not “persons within the jurisdiction” of the state of Texas; and therefore, were not entitled to equal protection under Texas law. The Court rejected this argument under the reasoning that, regardless of an individual's immigration status, an undocumented immigrant is a “person” in the ordinary sense of the word. The Court also noted that its prior precedent in Mathews v. Diaz, 426 U.S. 67 (1976), had already established that “aliens” including those who are unlawfully present, are “persons” entitled to constitutional protections, including the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment. After determining that undocumented immigrants are “persons within the jurisdiction” of Texas, the Court considered what level of constitutional scrutiny should apply.
